title: Offshore Accounting Without Losing Control of Quality
excerpt: The firms that get the most out of an offshore team are not the ones that hand over the most work — they are the ones that hand over the right work, with the right controls around it.
author: NUMETRIC Team
content:
Most partners we speak to have the same worry before their first engagement: *if I can't see the work being done, how do I know it's right?*

It is a fair question, and the answer is not "trust us". The answer is process.

## Start with the work that is already documented

The best first candidates for offshore delivery are the tasks your firm has already written down: bank reconciliations, month-end close checklists, payroll runs, fixed asset schedules. These have clear inputs, clear outputs, and an obvious definition of done.

Work that lives only in a senior manager's head is the *last* thing to move, not the first.

## Build a review layer, not a hand-off

A hand-off assumes the work leaves your firm and comes back finished. A review layer assumes something different: that every deliverable passes through a defined checkpoint before it reaches a client.

- Agree who signs off, and on what
- Define the sample size for spot checks in the first 90 days
- Log every exception, not just the ones that caused a problem
- Reduce the sample only when the exception rate justifies it

> The goal is not zero errors in month one. The goal is a falling error rate you can actually measure.

## Keep one system of record

The single biggest source of friction we see is duplicated state — a spreadsheet on your side, a different spreadsheet on ours. Pick one ledger, one document store, one place where the status of a job is true, and make both teams work inside it.

If your firm runs Xero, run the engagement in Xero. If time is tracked in BioLogs, track all of it there, including ours.

## Measure the right three things

After the first quarter, you only need three numbers to know whether the arrangement is working:

1. **Turnaround time** — from documents received to deliverable ready for review
2. **Exception rate** — items returned for correction, as a share of items delivered
3. **Partner hours recovered** — the whole point of the exercise

If turnaround is falling, exceptions are falling, and partner hours are being recovered, the model is working. If partner hours are not moving, you have moved the work but not the responsibility — and that is worth fixing before you scale it up.

title: A Month-End Close Checklist That Actually Holds Up
excerpt: Every firm has a close checklist. Most of them quietly stop reflecting reality within a year. Here is the structure we use to keep ours honest across four jurisdictions.
author: NUMETRIC Team
content:
A close checklist fails in a predictable way. Someone adds a step after a bad month, nobody ever removes a step, and eighteen months later the list is forty items long and half of them get ticked without being read.

Here is how we keep the structure tight.

## Group by dependency, not by account

Organising by account type feels natural and reconciles badly with how a close actually runs. Order the list by what blocks what:

1. **Inputs complete** — bank feeds, statements, payroll files, supplier invoices
2. **Transactions classified** — coding, accruals, prepayments, intercompany
3. **Accounts reconciled** — bank, credit card, control accounts, clearing accounts
4. **Schedules updated** — fixed assets, depreciation, leases, provisions
5. **Statements produced** — trial balance review, P&L, balance sheet, cash flow
6. **Reviewed and released** — variance commentary, sign-off, client delivery

A step in group four should never be attempted while group two is incomplete. Ordering by dependency makes that visible.

## Make every item falsifiable

"Review the balance sheet" is not a checklist item. It cannot be failed, so it cannot be verified.

"Every balance sheet account has a supporting schedule agreeing to the ledger, or a documented reason it does not" is a checklist item. Someone can look at it and say yes or no.

## Separate the jurisdictional layer

The core close is the same everywhere. What differs is the compliance overlay: `BAS` and superannuation in Australia, `VAT` and Making Tax Digital in the UK, `GST/PST` in Canada, multi-state payroll in the US.

Keep those as a separate appended block per entity rather than mixed into the core list. Otherwise every client's checklist becomes bespoke, and bespoke checklists do not survive staff turnover.

## Review the list quarterly, with deletions

Once a quarter, walk the list and ask two questions of every item:

- Has this ever caught anything?
- If we deleted it, what would go wrong?

Anything that fails both gets removed. A checklist that only ever grows is a checklist people stop reading.

title: What a Certified Xero Partner Actually Buys You
excerpt: Certification badges are easy to display and hard to interpret. Here is a practical read on what L1 and L2 Xero certification changes about day-to-day delivery.
author: NUMETRIC Team
content:
Plenty of providers list a Xero badge. Fewer can tell you what it changes about the work.

## What it does mean

Certification means the team has been assessed on the platform rather than self-taught around it. In practice that shows up in three places:

- **Chart of accounts design.** A well-structured chart set up at onboarding saves more time over a year than any amount of downstream tidying.
- **Bank rules and reconciliation.** Reconciliation is where most bookkeeping hours go. Rules that are written properly the first time convert a recurring manual task into an exception-only review.
- **Reporting layouts.** Custom report templates mean management packs are generated, not rebuilt each month.

## What it does not mean

It does not mean your jurisdiction's compliance is handled automatically. Xero will happily produce a compliant-looking report from non-compliant inputs. The standards knowledge — `FRS`, `AASB`, `ASPE`, `GAAP` — sits with the people, not the software.

It also does not mean migration is free of judgement calls. Opening balances, part-year comparatives and historical transaction depth all need deciding before a conversion, and those decisions are hard to unwind afterwards.

## The integration question

The compounding benefit shows up when Xero is not working alone. Time captured in a tracking tool and pushed through to invoice-ready data removes a re-keying step that is both slow and error-prone.

> Any step where a human retypes a number that a system already knows is a step worth removing.
